dom.t: Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability

st.t: Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability
st.an: Cosgrove directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It applies an objective reasonably prudent attorney standard, rejects subjective good faith as an excuse, and identifies duty, breach, proximate causation, injury and damages as distinct requirements. The supplied excerpts do not resolve ultimate recovery, but that limitation does not undermine the source’s support for the cluster.
qs: There is no subjective good faith excuse for attorney negligence.
The plaintiff must prove that there is a duty owed to him by the defendant, a breach of that duly, that the breach proximately caused the plaintiff injury and that damages occurred.

mo.t: Delegated error: Client relief need not excuse counsel
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Lawyer accountability: Discipline and liability remain separate
Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Subjective good faith does not excuse attorney negligence
kp.d: The Supreme Court of Texas rejects a subjective good-faith defense to legal malpractice and disapproves earlier Texas decisions recognizing that exception. The court reasons that allowing good intentions to excuse objectively unreasonable conduct places too great a burden on wronged clients.
qs: There is no subjective good faith excuse for attorney negligence.
To the extent that some Texas courts have recognized an exception to attorney negligence based on the subjective good faith of the attorney, those cases are disapproved.

kp.k: Professional judgment is assessed objectively using contemporaneous information
kp.d: The court holds attorneys to the care of a reasonably prudent attorney, assessed using information available at the time of the alleged negligence. Tactical and strategic choices fall within this objective standard rather than receiving a separate exemption based on the attorney's beliefs.
qs: A lawyer in Texas is held to the standard of care which would be exercised by a reasonably prudent attorney.
The jury must evaluate his conduct based on the information the attorney has at the time of the alleged act of negligence.
The standard is an objective exercise of professional judgment, not the subjective belief that his acts are in good faith.

kp.k: An undesirable result does not establish malpractice
kp.d: The court distinguishes negligent decisions from reasonable professional judgments that subsequently prove imperfect. Lawyers are not strictly liable for failing to fulfill client expectations; the relevant question is whether a reasonably prudent attorney could have made the decision in similar circumstances.
qs: Attorneys cannot be held strictly liable for all of their clients’ unfulfilled expectations.
An attorney who makes a reasonable decision in the handling of a case may not be held liable if the decision later proves to be imperfect.

kp.k: Malpractice requires duty, breach, causation and damages
kp.d: The opinion identifies negligence as the basis of a Texas attorney-malpractice action and sets out four required elements. In this case, the court finds record support for the jury's findings that Grimes negligently represented Cosgrove and that this failure adversely affected him.
qs: An attorney malpractice action in Texas is based on negligence.
An action for negligence is based on four elements.

The jury found in issue number 5 that Grimes had been negligent in his representation of Cosgrove and in issue number 6 that such negligence adversely affected Cosgrove. There is evidence in the record to support these findings.

kp.k: Reliance on client information did not defeat negligence findings
kp.d: Grimes sued the passenger rather than the driver before limitations expired and alleged an incorrect accident location. He asserted reliance on information supplied by Cosgrove; their accounts of when Grimes became involved differed. Although the jury found good-faith reliance and action in the client's best interest, the Supreme Court held that submitting those good-faith issues was error.
qs: Grimes, alleging that he had relied on Cosgrove’s information, had filed suit against the passenger in the car which struck Cosgrove, rather than Stephens, the car’s driver.
The jury found Grimes had in good faith relied on the information given to him by Cosgrove, and based upon that information, Grimes had acted in Cosgrove’s best interest.
We hold that the trial court erred in submitting issues to the jury concerning Grimes’ good faith.

kp.k: Recovery included lost collision damages and mental anguish
kp.d: The court rendered a $2500.00 award for Grimes' negligent prosecution: $2000 reflecting the underlying collision recovery and $500 for mental anguish caused by his representation. The underlying-damages questions should have addressed amounts recoverable and collectible had the suit been properly prosecuted, but Grimes waived their defects by failing to object distinctly. The court separately upheld the mental-anguish question as properly assessing damage from the negligent handling.
qs: Because Grimes waived the error in the submission, we render judgment that Cosgrove recover $2000 in accordance with the jury’s finding on issues number 7 and 8.
The jury found in response to issue number 9, that $500 would fairly and reasonably compensate Cosgrove for mental anguish suffered as a result of Grimes’ negligence.
This issue properly assessed damages incurred by Cosgrove because of Grimes’ negligent handling of the first suit.

kp.d: The court assumed only for argument that an implied-warranty claim against an attorney existed under the 1977 DTPA. It denied recovery on that theory because Cosgrove's submitted questions addressed care rather than breach of an implied warranty, and his failure to tender a properly worded question waived that ground of recovery.
qs: Assuming _arguendo_ such a cause of action existed against an attorney under the 1977 version of the DTPA, the issues requested by Cosgrove did not properly place the matter before the jury.
At best the language of the submission vaguely alluded to a standard of care, not to an implied warranty.
Because the issue did not inquire whether Grimes breached an implied warranty, Cosgrove may not recover on such a claim.
